name: Istanbul
tagline: Where two continents meet over tea, minarets and the Bosphorus
description:
Istanbul doesn't so much straddle two continents as stitch them together, one ferry crossing at a time. For roughly sixteen centuries it was an imperial capital, first Byzantine and then Ottoman, and the layers are everywhere: Hagia Sophia's floating dome, Sinan's mosques cascading towards the Golden Horn, Roman columns rising from a flooded cistern, and palaces that once ruled lands from the gates of Vienna to the Persian Gulf.

Yet this is a living megacity of some 16 million people, not an open-air museum. Simit sellers balance trays of sesame rings on their heads, anglers line the Galata Bridge, and the smoke of grilling mackerel drifts over Eminönü. Cross to Kadıköy on the Asian side for fish markets and buzzing bars, or lose an afternoon in Balat's tilted, candy-coloured streets.

Allow at least four days. Pair the big-ticket Sultanahmet sights with slower moments — tea on a Bosphorus terrace, a steamy hamam scrub, and a long night of rakı and meze in Beyoğlu, where the city hums until well past midnight.

safety.notes: Violent crime against tourists is rare, but pickpockets work crowded trams and İstiklal Avenue, and the old scam of a friendly stranger steering solo men to an overpriced bar still operates around Taksim and Sultanahmet. Use a taxi app or insist on the meter.

tipping: Leave around 10% in restaurants (in cash if you can), round up taxi fares, and tip hamam attendants 10–15%.
gettingAround: Load an Istanbulkart for trams, metro, the Marmaray tunnel, funiculars and ferries; the T1 tram links Sultanahmet with Eminönü and Karaköy, and public ferries are the cheapest, most scenic way to hop between continents.
tips: Visit mosques outside the five daily prayer times and avoid Friday midday entirely, when congregations fill every space.
Skip pricey private cruises and ride the public ferry from Eminönü to Kadıköy or Üsküdar for Bosphorus views at a fraction of the cost.
One Istanbulkart can be tapped for several people in turn, so a group only needs one card topped up with enough credit.
Pay in Turkish lira rather than euros or dollars — prices quoted in foreign currency almost always hide a poor exchange rate.
In the Grand Bazaar, compare prices at several shops before haggling and walk away politely if the number feels wrong; the best offer often comes as you leave.
Hagia Sophia's tourist route leads to the upper galleries while the ground floor is reserved for worshippers — arrive before 09:00 to dodge the longest queues.
etiquette: In mosques, remove your shoes, cover shoulders and knees, and women should cover their hair — scarves are usually lent at the door.
Accepting a glass of tea from a shopkeeper is simple hospitality, not a commitment to buy.
Insulting Atatürk or the Turkish flag is a criminal offence, and even light-hearted jokes can cause real offence.
Never walk directly in front of someone praying, and keep voices and camera shutters low inside religious sites.

neighborhoods.name: Sultanahmet
neighborhoods.blurb: The historic peninsula's showpiece, with Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque and Topkapı Palace within a few hundred metres of each other. Convenient, though quiet and touristy after dark.

neighborhoods.name: Karaköy
neighborhoods.blurb: A former port and banking district whose grand old buildings now house third-wave cafés, galleries and design hotels, a short stroll downhill from Galata Tower.

neighborhoods.name: Beyoğlu
neighborhoods.blurb: The city's European-style heart around İstiklal Avenue, with 19th-century arcades, rooftop bars, meyhanes and live-music clubs that rarely close before dawn.

neighborhoods.name: Balat
neighborhoods.blurb: A hilly quarter on the Golden Horn shaped by Jewish, Greek and Armenian heritage, now famous for its colourful houses, antique shops and quirky cafés.

neighborhoods.name: Kadıköy
neighborhoods.blurb: The Asian side's buzzing hub, with a sprawling food market, craft-beer bars and a young, creative crowd — just a 20-minute ferry ride from Europe.

dishes.name: Kahvaltı
dishes.description: The epic Turkish breakfast spread: cheeses, olives, tomatoes, cucumbers, honey with clotted kaymak, eggs with spicy sucuk and bottomless glasses of tea.

dishes.name: Balık ekmek
dishes.description: A grilled mackerel fillet stuffed into crusty bread with onion and lettuce, sold from boats and stalls along the Eminönü waterfront.

dishes.name: Midye dolma
dishes.description: Mussels stuffed with spiced rice, pine nuts and currants, sold by the handful from street trays and eaten with a squeeze of lemon.

dishes.name: Rakı and meze
dishes.description: The aniseed spirit that clouds milky-white with water, sipped slowly over a parade of cold and hot small plates — Istanbul's great social ritual.

dishes.name: Künefe
dishes.description: Shredded kadayıf pastry layered with stretchy unsalted cheese, baked crisp, soaked in syrup and showered with pistachio — best eaten piping hot.

events.name: Istanbul Tulip Festival
events.description: Millions of tulips carpet Emirgan Park, Gülhane Park and roadside verges across the city, celebrating the flower the Ottomans made famous.

events.name: Istanbul Music Festival
events.description: Classical concerts, opera and recitals staged in atmospheric venues, from historic churches to palace halls.

events.name: Istanbul Jazz Festival
events.description: Jazz, soul and world-music headliners play open-air stages, parks and intimate clubs across the city.

events.name: Istanbul Marathon
events.description: The only major marathon that crosses continents, starting on the Asian side and racing over the Bosphorus bridge into Europe.

attractions.name: Hagia Sophia
attractions.description: Completed as a Byzantine cathedral in 537, later a mosque, then a museum and now a mosque again, this is one of the most influential buildings ever raised. Visitors tour the upper galleries, where golden mosaics of Christ and emperors gaze across a dome that seems to float on a ring of light.
attractions.hours: Visitor galleries roughly 09:00–19:30 daily; closed during Friday midday prayers
attractions.bookingTip: Foreign visitors need a ticket for the separate gallery route; arrive before 09:00 or late afternoon to avoid hour-long lines.

attractions.name: Blue Mosque
attractions.description: Six slender minarets and a cascade of domes announce the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, whose interior shimmers with more than 20,000 hand-painted İznik tiles in blues and greens. It remains an active place of worship, so visits pause for each of the five daily prayers.
attractions.hours: Open daily outside prayer times; closed to visitors until mid-afternoon on Fridays
attractions.bookingTip: Use the visitors' entrance and check the posted prayer schedule — arriving about 30 minutes after a prayer ends is ideal.

attractions.name: Topkapı Palace
attractions.description: For nearly four centuries this sprawling complex of courtyards, kiosks and pavilions was the nerve centre of the Ottoman Empire. Don't miss the Harem's tiled chambers, the Treasury's 86-carat Spoonmaker's Diamond and the marble terraces overlooking the meeting of the Bosphorus and the Golden Horn.
attractions.hours: 09:00–18:00 Wed–Mon (closed Tue); to about 16:45 in winter
attractions.bookingTip: Buy tickets online and head straight for the Harem, which gets packed by late morning.

attractions.name: Basilica Cistern
attractions.description: Descend into a sixth-century underground reservoir where 336 marble columns rise from shallow water in moody amber light. Seek out the two upside-down and sideways Medusa heads recycled as column bases in the far corner.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy online and go at opening; by midday the line along the street can stretch for an hour.

attractions.name: Grand Bazaar
attractions.description: One of the world's oldest covered markets is a labyrinth of some 60 lanes and thousands of shops selling carpets, lanterns, leather, ceramics and gold. Look up at the painted vaults, and slip into the hidden han courtyards where artisans still hammer silver.
attractions.bookingTip: Enter through the Nuruosmaniye Gate early in the morning, when shopkeepers are sipping tea and happier to chat than hard-sell.

attractions.name: Spice Bazaar
attractions.description: This 17th-century L-shaped market overflows with pyramids of spices, dried fruit, Turkish delight and loose-leaf teas. The lanes just outside, where locals actually buy cheese, olives and freshly ground coffee, are even more atmospheric.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy spices from the shops outside the main hall, where prices are lower and turnover — and freshness — is higher.

attractions.name: Süleymaniye Mosque
attractions.description: Mimar Sinan's 16th-century masterpiece crowns the Third Hill with serene proportions and a courtyard far calmer than Sultanahmet's. Walk round to the rear terrace for one of the city's finest free views over the Golden Horn.
attractions.hours: Open daily outside prayer times, roughly 09:00 to dusk
attractions.bookingTip: Pair your visit with lunch at the bean-stew canteens lining the street beside the mosque.

attractions.name: Galata Tower
attractions.description: This stout 14th-century Genoese tower rises above the rooftops of Galata, and its narrow wraparound balcony delivers a 360-degree panorama of minarets, bridges and ferries criss-crossing the water. The lanes below are full of cafés and musical-instrument shops.
attractions.bookingTip: Join the queue about an hour before sunset, or go right at opening for the shortest wait and soft morning light.

attractions.name: Dolmabahçe Palace
attractions.description: The sultans' 19th-century answer to Versailles stretches along the Bosphorus shore, dripping with crystal chandeliers, gold leaf and a staircase with crystal balusters. Atatürk died here in 1938, and the palace clocks are still stopped at 9:05.
attractions.bookingTip: Daily visitor numbers are capped, so arrive early and allow time for the separate Harem section.

attractions.name: İstiklal Avenue
attractions.description: This pedestrian boulevard runs from Taksim Square towards Galata, lined with belle-époque arcades, churches and bookshops, with side streets packed with meyhanes and rooftop bars. The little red heritage tram rattles down the middle, and crowds peak on weekend nights.
attractions.bookingTip: Duck into the side streets of Asmalımescit for dinner — the restaurants right on the main drag are overpriced.

hotels.name: Yalı Selvinaz Bosphorus Palace
hotels.description: A restored Ottoman waterside mansion with its own jetty, where suites open onto the Bosphorus and ships glide past close enough to wave at. A marble hamam and a private guest boat for dinners along the shore complete the fantasy.

hotels.name: Nar Çiçeği Konak
hotels.description: Eleven rooms in a painted wooden Ottoman townhouse on a cobbled lane behind the Blue Mosque, furnished with kilims and hammered-copper basins. The rooftop breakfast of village cheeses and honeycomb comes with a minaret-level view.

hotels.name: Çay Ocağı Hostel
hotels.description: Named after the tiny tea stands that fuel Istanbul, this sociable hostel pours free tea all day and has a rooftop terrace overlooking the Golden Horn. Dorms come with privacy curtains and lockers, and staff lead evening walks to cheap meyhanes.

hotels.name: Pervane Design Hotel
hotels.description: An 1890s apartment block reborn with terrazzo floors, brass fittings and bold contemporary Turkish art on every landing. The rooftop cocktail bar looks across Cihangir's rooftops to the Bosphorus.

hotels.name: Eski Kütüphane Hotel
hotels.description: Once home to a family of Ottoman scholars, this restored stone mansion keeps its arched rooms, carved wooden bookcases and a trickling courtyard fountain. Mornings begin with the call to prayer echoing off Sinan's domes next door.

hotels.name: Bakırcı Loft Apartments
hotels.description: Spacious lofts with full kitchens and washing machines on a coppersmiths' street just outside the Grand Bazaar's gates. Ideal for families or longer stays, with the tram stop two minutes' walk away.

restaurants.name: Balıkçı Nuri'nin Teknesi
restaurants.description: A gently rocking boat moored at the Eminönü quay, where Nuri and his sons grill mackerel over roaring flames and pass it ashore stuffed into bread. Grab a low stool, add a cup of pickle juice from the next stall and watch the ferries come and go.

restaurants.name: Bal & Kaymak Kahvaltı Evi
restaurants.description: A family-run breakfast house serving serpme kahvaltı — a table-covering spread of cheeses, olives, jams, clotted kaymak with honeycomb and menemen bubbling in a copper pan. Arrive hungry and linger over endless glasses of tea.
restaurants.signatureDish: Serpme kahvaltı with honeycomb and kaymak

restaurants.name: Şerbetçibaşı
restaurants.description: Named after the palace's chief sherbet-maker, this elegant dining room revives recipes from old Ottoman kitchen ledgers — lamb with quince, almond soup, rose-scented sherbets — as a refined tasting menu. Terrace tables look across the water to the Asian shore.

restaurants.name: Meyhane Üç Kadeh
restaurants.description: Cold mezes arrive on a tray for you to point and pick, followed by hot plates like crisp calamari and grilled octopus, all washed down with rakı. By 11pm a fasıl band is weaving between tables and strangers are singing along.

restaurants.name: Usta Rıfat Esnaf Lokantası
restaurants.description: Point at steaming trays of stews, stuffed peppers and buttery pilaf in this no-menu workers' canteen, where shopkeepers from the surrounding lanes have lunched for decades. Portions are generous, prices tiny, and most trays are empty by 3pm.
restaurants.signatureDish: Kuru fasulye (white bean stew) with pilaf

restaurants.name: Ocakbaşı Kırmızı Biber
restaurants.description: Grab a seat at the copper-hooded grill and watch the usta sear Adana kebab, lamb ribs and chicken wings over charcoal, handing them over on thin lavaş with sumac onions. Students and football fans pack it on match nights.

restaurants.name: Tiflis Hinkali Evi
restaurants.description: Juicy soup dumplings, boat-shaped khachapuri with a runny egg and walnut-rich pkhali make this cosy Georgian kitchen a warming detour. Order a glass of amber clay-pot wine to go with it.

restaurants.name: Fıstık Ustası
restaurants.description: Trays of glistening pistachio baklava fill the window, but the real draw is künefe baked to order in small copper pans and served molten. Pair it with a Turkish coffee or a tulip glass of tea.

experiences.name: Two-Continent Sunset Sail on a Wooden Yacht
experiences.description: Board a restored wooden motor yacht near Kabataş and cruise past Ottoman palaces, waterside mansions and fortress walls as the sun sets behind the minarets. A light meze plate and drinks are served on deck.
includes: Tea, soft drinks and a glass of wine

experiences.name: Ferry-to-Kadıköy Street-Food Crawl
experiences.description: Start among the spice sacks of Eminönü, then ride the public ferry to the Asian side for a grazing walk through Kadıköy's market lanes, sampling stuffed mussels, lahmacun, pickles, Turkish delight and syrupy desserts. With around 15 tastings, skip lunch.

experiences.name: Traditional Hamam Ritual with Kese Scrub
experiences.description: Unwind on the heated marble navel stone of a domed bathhouse near the Süleymaniye complex, then surrender to a vigorous kese exfoliation and a cloud of olive-oil soap foam. Sessions are single-gender, with female attendants for women.

experiences.name: Home-Style Meze and Dolma Cooking Class
experiences.description: Cook with an Istanbul home chef in her Galata apartment, learning to roll vine-leaf dolma, whip up garlicky cacık and bake flaky börek. The session ends around her table with everything you've made and a glass of Turkish wine or ayran.
includes: Lunch of the dishes you make
